Removing is destructive — data is gone unless you've taken a backup:

scalingo --app my-app addons-remove <addon-id>

PostgreSQL

Scalingo for PostgreSQL® — the most full-featured database on the platform.

Provider ID: postgresql. Connection env var: SCALINGO_POSTGRESQL_URL, also aliased to DATABASE_URL.

scalingo --app my-app addons-add postgresql postgresql-starter-512

Plan naming: postgresql-starter-<RAM in MB> (512, 1024, 2048, ...) and postgresql-business-<RAM in MB> (1024 and up).

Versions: PostgreSQL 14 to 18 are supported; new addons default to 17. PostgreSQL 14 reaches end of life on 2026-11-12, and remaining 14 databases are upgraded to 15 automatically on 2027-01-11 — upgrade on your own schedule before that.

Key features:

  • Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR) on all plans (7-day window on shared resources)
  • High availability on Business: 1 primary + 1 standby. The standby is for failover only and is not exposed for connections — there are no read-only replicas
  • pg_stat_statements, pg_trgm, PostGIS available (enable extensions with CREATE EXTENSION)
  • Major version upgrades via dashboard (one-click)
  • TLS is available on every plan; forcing it is an optional toggle on any plan (database-enable-feature force-ssl)

Connect from a one-off:

scalingo --app my-app pgsql-console
# or inside `scalingo run bash`:
dbclient-fetcher postgresql
psql $SCALINGO_POSTGRESQL_URL

MySQL

Provider ID: mysql. Env var: SCALINGO_MYSQL_URL (and DATABASE_URL alias for single-DB setups).

scalingo --app my-app addons-add mysql mysql-starter-512

MySQL 8.4 is the current version; remaining 8.0 databases were upgraded to 8.4 automatically on 2026-10-12. The mysql-console CLI one-off and dbclient-fetcher mysql work as for PostgreSQL.

MongoDB

Provider ID: mongodb. Env var: SCALINGO_MONGO_URL, aliased to MONGO_URL and MONGODB_URI depending on app conventions.

scalingo --app my-app addons-add mongodb mongo-starter-512

Plans follow the same pattern; the smallest MongoDB plan is 256 MB. Business tier provides a 3-node replica set for HA. Since CLI 1.50.0, mongo-console uses mongosh.

Connect:

scalingo --app my-app mongo-console
# or
dbclient-fetcher mongo
mongosh $SCALINGO_MONGO_URL

Scalingo for Caching (Redis)

Renamed from "Scalingo for Redis" to Scalingo for Caching in June 2025 for trademark reasons. The engine is still Redis OSS (7.2 by default, 6.2 available) and the provider ID is still redis. Env var: SCALINGO_REDIS_URL, often aliased to REDIS_URL.

scalingo --app my-app addons-add redis redis-starter-256   # smallest plan is 256 MB

Uses:

  • Session store
  • Job queue backend (Sidekiq, Celery, BullMQ)
  • Cache layer
  • Rate limiting

Business-tier plans run 3 nodes and provide persistent storage and replication. Starter plans are single-node and should not be the sole persistence layer for durable data.

scalingo --app my-app redis-console

OpenSearch

Provider ID: opensearch. Env var: SCALINGO_OPENSEARCH_URL (check scalingo env after attaching). Launched in June 2025 as the replacement for Elasticsearch.

scalingo --app my-app addons-add opensearch opensearch-starter-1024   # smallest plan is 1 GB

Backups of OpenSearch (and Elasticsearch) databases can't be downloaded.

Use for full-text search, log analytics, or vector search (with the k-NN plugin on supported plans). Connect via HTTP using the URL directly — credentials are embedded.

InfluxDB

Provider ID: influxdb. Env var: SCALINGO_INFLUX_URL.

Time-series data — metrics, IoT, sensor data. Connect with the InfluxDB client tooling using the URL and token from env, or scalingo --app my-app influxdb-console. InfluxDB is sold in the Starter class only (from 512 MB).

Elasticsearch (phasing out)

Scalingo is gradually phasing out Elasticsearch in favour of OpenSearch. Don't provision new Elasticsearch addons; plan a migration to OpenSearch for existing ones.

Backups

All managed databases take daily automated backups. Scheduled backup retention:

ClassDailyWeeklyMonthly
Starter74—
Business7812

Manual backups are capped (10 on Starter, 50 on Business). After a database is deleted, its manual backups are kept 1 month (Starter) or 1 year (Business).

scalingo --app my-app --addon <addon-id> backups                  # list
scalingo --app my-app --addon <addon-id> backups-create           # trigger one
scalingo --app my-app --addon <addon-id> backups-download --backup <backup-id>
scalingo --app my-app --addon <addon-id> backups-config --schedule-at 3   # daily backup hour

For PostgreSQL, Point-in-Time Recovery is available on every plan. The recovery window is 7 days on shared resources (7/14/30 days for Starter/Business/Enterprise on Dedicated Resources). Restore from the dashboard or the CLI:

scalingo --app my-app --addon postgresql database-pitr-recovery-window
scalingo --app my-app --addon postgresql database-pitr-restore 2026-07-18T23:00:00Z

Export to external storage (S3, etc.) is your responsibility; scripts running as detached one-offs are a common pattern:

scalingo --app my-app run --detached bash -c 'pg_dump $DATABASE_URL | gzip | aws s3 cp - s3://bucket/backup.sql.gz'

Service classes and sizing

Three service classes:

ClassArchitectureSLAUse case
StarterSingle node98%Dev, staging, small prod
BusinessPostgreSQL: 1 primary + 1 standby; Caching, MongoDB, OpenSearch: 3 nodes99.96%Production with HA requirements
Enterprise1 primary + 2 standbys99.99%Critical workloads (Dedicated Resources PostgreSQL only)

Dedicated Resources is not a class but an architecture model (see below); it offers Starter, Business, and Enterprise.

All tiers are managed (no OS access, no manual patching). Billing is per minute based on the current plan.

Sizing starts at 256 MB (Caching, MongoDB), 512 MB (PostgreSQL, MySQL, InfluxDB), or 1 GB (OpenSearch). Public pricing for shared resources goes up to 128 GB (PostgreSQL Business); larger sizes are on request. For guidance, ask:

  1. Working-set size — does it fit in RAM? That's the primary memory metric.
  2. Connection count — PostgreSQL's pgBouncer availability depends on plan.
  3. Write throughput — Starter's IO is best-effort; Business allocates dedicated IOPS.

Switch classes in minutes — moving from a single-node Starter to a multi-node Business plan (or back) is a supported upgrade path without downtime on HA-capable tiers.

Shared infrastructure vs dedicated

  • Shared Resources — dedicated instance (your own engine process, isolated data) on shared underlying infrastructure. This is the default for all Starter and Business plans. Suitable from dev through production.
  • Dedicated Resources — dedicated VMs and a dedicated VPC spread over up to 3 availability zones. PostgreSQL only, still in preview and available on request. A Dedicated Resources database is not attached to an app: only the owner can create it, it can only be scaled up, and logical backups are the customer's responsibility. CLI commands use --database <id> instead of --app/--addon and need SCALINGO_PREVIEW_FEATURES=true; Terraform uses scalingo_database. Outscale Net Peering is supported.

Architecture and networking

  • All addons run in the same region as their app for low latency
  • Connections go through an addon-specific hostname (embedded in the URL)
  • For most engines, plain TCP over the public internet is supported but TLS is available and recommended
  • Forcing TLS is opt-in on every plan (force-ssl feature)
  • No private networking between app and addon in Starter tier — traffic is internal to the region but not on a private VLAN
  • Dedicated Resources tier provides private networking

Migration and import

Into Scalingo

For PostgreSQL, the canonical path is pg_dump/pg_restore. From a machine with network access to both source and destination:

# Dump from source (Heroku example)
pg_dump $(heroku config:get DATABASE_URL -a old-app) > dump.sql

# Restore to Scalingo
scalingo --app new-app pgsql-console < dump.sql
# or via a one-off:
scalingo --app new-app run --size XL bash
# inside: curl dump-url | psql $DATABASE_URL

For MongoDB: mongodump / mongorestore. For MySQL: mysqldump / mysql. The dbclient-fetcher helper makes these tools available inside one-off containers.

Out of Scalingo

Backups are downloadable as archive files; contents are standard dumps compatible with the engine's native restore tools.

Log drains for addon logs

Addon logs (query logs, slow queries, replication events) can be drained separately from app logs:

scalingo --app my-app log-drains-add \
  --addon <addon-id> \
  --type syslog \
  --host logs.example.com --port 6514

scalingo --app my-app log-drains --with-addons   # list app and addon drains

Only database addons produce logs.

Useful for compliance — sending PostgreSQL audit logs to a long-term store.

Non-database addons

The platform supports various non-database addons (Mailgun, Papertrail, Sentry, Redsmin, Bugsnag, and others). They're discovered via:

scalingo addons-list

Attach and use env vars the provider defines. For details on any specific one, use addons-plans <provider> and the provider's own docs.

documents.label: Buildpacks and the Scalingo Stack
documents.html:
Buildpacks and the Scalingo Stack

Scalingo uses buildpacks — the same open-source ecosystem Heroku pioneered — to detect your app's stack, install dependencies, and produce a runnable slug. For most apps, detection is automatic and you never touch this. When it matters: a non-standard runtime, native dependencies, polyglot apps, or a custom build step.

The stack

The stack is the Ubuntu-based base image your buildpack runs against. The stack is pinned at app-creation time.

StackBaseStatus
scalingo-26Ubuntu 26.04Default since 2026-06-22, supported until May 2031
scalingo-24Ubuntu 24.04Supported until May 2029
scalingo-22Ubuntu 22.04Deprecated; discontinued on 2027-06-01 — migrate now
scalingo-20Ubuntu 20.04Discontinued in April 2025

List stacks and change one with:

scalingo stacks
scalingo --app my-app stacks-set scalingo-26   # takes effect on the next deploy

Stack images are public on Docker Hub as scalingo/scalingo-26, scalingo/scalingo-24, and scalingo/scalingo-22 (plus -minimal variants) — useful for local testing of buildpacks or reproducing build environments:

docker run --rm -it \
  -e STACK=scalingo-26 \
  -v "$(pwd):/build" \
  scalingo/scalingo-26:latest bash

Officially supported buildpacks (auto-detected)

Language/frameworkDetection signal
RubyGemfile
Pythonrequirements.txt, Pipfile, pyproject.toml, setup.py
Node.jspackage.json
PHPcomposer.json
Gogo.mod (or Godeps/)
Javapom.xml, build.gradle, *.jar
Elixirmix.exs
Clojureproject.clj
Scalabuild.sbt
Meteor.meteor/
StaticStaticfile

If multiple signals exist, the first match in detection order wins. To override, use a custom or multi buildpack (see below).

How detection picks a runtime version

Each buildpack reads the language-standard version file:

  • Node.js — "engines": { "node": "20.x" } in package.json, or .nvmrc
  • Python — runtime.txt (one line: python-3.12.7)
  • Ruby — ruby "3.2.2" directive in Gemfile
  • PHP — "require": { "php": "^8.2" } in composer.json
  • Java — system.properties file with java.runtime.version=21
  • Go — go.mod's go 1.22 directive

Pin these in your repo. Relying on defaults means silent upgrades when buildpacks update.

Forcing a specific buildpack

Set the BUILDPACK_URL env var before deploying:

scalingo --app my-app env-set BUILDPACK_URL=https://github.com/Scalingo/rust-buildpack
scalingo --app my-app deployment-delete-cache
git push scalingo main

Use this when:

  • The auto-detected buildpack is wrong (e.g. a repo has both package.json and Gemfile and you want Ruby)
  • You need a community buildpack (Rust, Crystal, Deno, Bun, Nim, ...)
  • You maintain your own buildpack for a non-standard runtime

Multi buildpack (polyglot apps)

A single build that runs multiple buildpacks in order — useful when a Python app needs Node.js for frontend assets:

scalingo --app my-app env-set BUILDPACK_URL=https://github.com/Scalingo/multi-buildpack

Then create a .buildpacks file at repo root:

https://github.com/Scalingo/nodejs-buildpack
https://github.com/Scalingo/python-buildpack

Buildpacks run top-to-bottom. The last buildpack determines the process types (the Procfile-derived ones), so order the runtime that provides the web server last.

Custom buildpacks

A buildpack is a git repo with three scripts:

bin/
├── detect      # Exit 0 if this buildpack applies
├── compile     # Install dependencies, compile the app
└── release     # Print YAML describing addons/env/default-Procfile

bin/detect

Takes a build directory as argument. Non-zero exit = skip this buildpack:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
if [ -f "$1/Cargo.toml" ]; then
  echo "Rust"
  exit 0
fi
exit 1

bin/compile

Takes BUILD_DIR, CACHE_DIR, ENV_DIR as arguments. Does the work:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
BUILD_DIR=$1
CACHE_DIR=$2

cd "$BUILD_DIR"
# Install Rust toolchain if not cached
if [ ! -d "$CACHE_DIR/rustup" ]; then
  curl -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | RUSTUP_HOME=$CACHE_DIR/rustup sh -s -- -y
fi
export PATH="$CACHE_DIR/rustup/bin:$PATH"

cargo build --release
mkdir -p "$BUILD_DIR/bin"
cp target/release/my-app "$BUILD_DIR/bin/"

At the end, the contents of BUILD_DIR are moved to /app in the final slug.

bin/release

Prints YAML metadata — addons, config vars, default Procfile entries. Applied only on first deploy:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
cat <<EOF
---
addons:
  - scalingo-postgresql
config_vars:
  PATH: /app/bin:/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin
default_process_types:
  web: /app/bin/my-app
EOF

If default_process_types is provided, users don't need a Procfile. If omitted, they do.

.profile.d/

Scripts dropped in .profile.d/ by buildpacks are sourced at container startup — used to set env vars that depend on runtime state (e.g. compiler paths). Don't write user scripts here; use .profile at repo root for app-specific init.

Testing a custom buildpack locally

# Get the stack image
docker pull scalingo/scalingo-26

# Mount the buildpack and the app, run the three scripts manually
docker run --rm -it \
  -e STACK=scalingo-26 \
  -v /path/to/my-buildpack:/buildpack \
  -v /path/to/my-app:/build \
  scalingo/scalingo-26:latest bash

# Inside the container:
/buildpack/bin/detect /build      # Should exit 0
/buildpack/bin/compile /build /cache /env
/buildpack/bin/release /build

Once the buildpack works, push it to a public git host and set BUILDPACK_URL.

Common buildpack patterns

Install a system package

Use the apt buildpack (Scalingo maintains a fork):

scalingo --app my-app env-set BUILDPACK_URL=https://github.com/Scalingo/multi-buildpack

.buildpacks:

https://github.com/Scalingo/apt-buildpack
https://github.com/Scalingo/python-buildpack

Aptfile at repo root:

imagemagick
libpq-dev
ffmpeg

Packages are installed into /app/.apt and added to PATH/LD_LIBRARY_PATH.

Use a specific Node version not in the default list

The Node buildpack respects engines.node in package.json. Pin "node": "20.11.1" for exact version, "20.x" for latest 20.

Python with C extensions

requirements.txt with packages like psycopg2-binary, Pillow, lxml usually "just works" on scalingo-26. For packages needing build-time system headers, add an Aptfile with -dev packages and use the multi buildpack with apt first.

Compile-once binaries

For languages like Rust or Go where the build output is a single binary, consider the archive deploy method: build in CI (against the same stack image), then deploy a tarball with the binary and a minimal Procfile. Archive deploys still run a buildpack build, so this only skips compilation if the buildpack you use accepts a prebuilt binary.

Private buildpacks

BUILDPACK_URL accepts any git URL. For a private repo, use the HTTPS form with an access token in the URL (less secure) or host on an internal git server reachable from Scalingo. SSH-based private git URLs aren't supported for buildpacks.

Build failures — triage order

  1. Check scalingo logs during the build — the buildpack prints what it's doing
  2. Verify the detected buildpack matches your expectation (first line of build output: -----> Detected buildpack: X)
  3. If a dependency install fails, check if the version is too new/old for the stack — pin explicitly
  4. If a native build fails, check whether the needed system package is present (use apt buildpack if not)
  5. If everything looks right but fails: clear the cache (scalingo deployment-delete-cache) and retry
  6. Reproduce locally in the Docker image of your app's stack (e.g. scalingo/scalingo-26)
  7. If the build is killed, check the limits: 30 minutes, 6 CPUs / 8 GB build container, 2 GiB image

Common specific errors:

  • Could not determine Ruby version → add ruby "3.2.2" to Gemfile
  • No such file or directory: pip → the Python buildpack didn't detect; check for requirements.txt / Pipfile
  • Error while executing gyp → a native Node dependency; may need the apt buildpack for build-essential, or prefer prebuilt wheels
  • heroku- prefix on a community buildpack URL → Scalingo's buildpacks are usually at github.com/Scalingo/...-buildpack; Heroku buildpacks mostly work but may reference Heroku-specific paths

documents.label: Scalingo CLI Reference
documents.html:
Scalingo CLI Reference

Complete command map for the scalingo CLI. Install with:

curl -O https://cli-dl.scalingo.com/install && bash install

All commands that act on an app accept --app <name> or -a <name>. Commands that act across regions accept --region <region> (or use the default set by scalingo config --region).

Table of contents

  1. Global
  2. Apps (incl. Projects and private networks)
  3. Deployment and Git
  4. Process types and scaling
  5. One-off containers
  6. Environment variables
  7. Addons
  8. Database helpers
  9. Domains and TLS
  10. Logs
  11. Collaborators and access
  12. SCM integrations and review apps
  13. Events and audit
  14. Stats and metrics
  15. Addon configuration
  16. Firewall, output format, and preview features

Global

scalingo login                       # Browser-based login
scalingo logout
scalingo self                        # Show the logged-in user
scalingo regions                     # List regions (osc-fr1, osc-secnum-fr1, ...)
scalingo config --region osc-fr1     # Set default region
scalingo help <command>              # Per-command help
scalingo --version

Environment-based auth for CI:

export SCALINGO_API_TOKEN=tk-us-...
export SCALINGO_REGION=osc-fr1

Generate an API token in the dashboard: Account Settings → API Tokens.

Apps

scalingo apps                        # List your apps in the current region
scalingo create <name>               # Create an app (validates name uniqueness)
scalingo create <name> --project-id <project-id>   # Create inside a project
scalingo --app <name> stacks-set scalingo-26       # Pin a stack (there is no `create --stack`)
scalingo rename --app old --new-name new
scalingo destroy --app <name>        # Delete (requires typing the app name)
scalingo --app <name> apps-info      # Metadata (region, stack, status)

create only accepts --remote, --buildpack, --project-id, and --hds-resource. Set the stack afterwards with stacks-set (available stacks: scalingo stacks).

Projects and private networks

Projects group apps; Private Networks are attached to a project and let its apps reach each other without going through the public internet.

scalingo projects                    # List projects (see `scalingo help` for the projects-* family)
scalingo --app <name> project-set <project-id>     # Move an app into a project
scalingo --app <name> private-networks-domain-names   # Private DNS names of the app's containers

Deployment and Git

scalingo --app <name> git-show       # Show the git remote URL for the app
scalingo --app <name> git-setup      # Add the `scalingo` remote to local repo

# Archive deploy: local tar.gz (or WAR) path, or a URL reachable from the platform.
# The archive must contain the code inside a single top-level folder (any name).
scalingo --app <name> deploy my-app.tar.gz
scalingo --app <name> deploy <https://.../archive.tar.gz>
scalingo --app <name> deploy <https://.../archive.tar.gz> <git-ref>

# Reset build cache (forces buildpack to run fresh)
scalingo --app <name> deployment-delete-cache

# Deployments list and status
scalingo --app <name> deployments
scalingo --app <name> deployment-follow <deployment-id>

Process types and scaling

Scale uses the syntax <process>:<amount>:<size>. Size is optional and keeps the current value.

scalingo --app <name> ps             # Show formation
scalingo --app <name> scale web:2:L              # 2 web containers at L
scalingo --app <name> scale worker:1:M web:3     # Multiple types at once
scalingo --app <name> scale worker:0              # Stop a process type
scalingo --app <name> restart                    # All containers
scalingo --app <name> restart web                # One process type

Container sizes (memory / CPU priority):

SizeMemoryCPU priority
S256 MBlow
M512 MBstandard (default)
L1 GBstandard
XL2 GBhigh
2XL4 GBhigh
3XL8 GBhigh

3XL is the largest size and is self-service. A process type can run up to 10 containers by default.

Autoscaler commands are keyed by container type, not by an ID:

scalingo --app <name> autoscalers
scalingo --app <name> autoscalers-add -c web -m cpu -t 0.75 --min-containers 2 --max-containers 10
scalingo --app <name> autoscalers-update -c web -t 0.6
scalingo --app <name> autoscalers-disable web
scalingo --app <name> autoscalers-enable web
scalingo --app <name> autoscalers-remove web

See scaling-autoscaler.md for metric names and targets.

One-off containers

One-offs are ephemeral copies of your production environment. The number of concurrent one-offs is limited per app and per account.

# Attached (interactive, closed after 30 min with no data exchanged)
scalingo --app <name> run bash
scalingo --app <name> run --size XL python manage.py migrate
scalingo --app <name> run --env DEBUG=1 --env FOO=bar bash

# Detached (runs without a terminal; you must ensure it exits)
scalingo --app <name> run --detached long-job.sh

# List and stop detached one-offs
scalingo --app <name> ps
scalingo --app <name> one-off-stop <one-off-id>

Any one-off (attached or detached) is killed after 1 hour without producing output, so long jobs should log progress.

Environment variables

scalingo --app <name> env            # Show all (values visible)
scalingo --app <name> env-get KEY    # Single value
scalingo --app <name> env-set KEY=value KEY2=value2
scalingo --app <name> env-unset KEY KEY2

Env changes do not restart the app — batch and then scalingo restart.

Limits: 64 chars for name, 32,768 chars for value.

For multi-line secrets, either quote carefully on the CLI or Base64-encode:

scalingo --app <name> env-set "PRIVATE_KEY=$(cat key.pem | base64 -w 0)"
# then decode in-app

Addons

# Discovery
scalingo addons-list                            # List all available addon providers
scalingo addons-plans <provider-id>              # Plans for a given provider

# Lifecycle
scalingo --app <name> addons                     # List attached addons
scalingo --app <name> addons-add <provider> <plan>
scalingo --app <name> addons-info <addon-id>
scalingo --app <name> addons-upgrade <addon-id> <new-plan>
scalingo --app <name> addons-remove <addon-id>

# Example: attach a PostgreSQL database
scalingo --app my-api addons-add postgresql postgresql-starter-512

Attached addon IDs look like ad-<uuid>. Connection info is injected as env (e.g. SCALINGO_POSTGRESQL_URL), with DATABASE_URL set as an alias for single-database setups.

Database helpers

Built-in REPL one-offs. They figure out credentials from env and open the right client:

scalingo --app <name> pgsql-console
scalingo --app <name> mysql-console
scalingo --app <name> mongo-console      # uses mongosh since CLI 1.50.0
scalingo --app <name> redis-console
scalingo --app <name> influxdb-console
scalingo --app <name> valkey-console

Inside a one-off bash, install CLI tools for your addon with:

dbclient-fetcher postgresql
dbclient-fetcher mysql 8.4
dbclient-fetcher mongo
dbclient-fetcher redis

Backup management (database commands take the addon with --addon <addon-id>):

scalingo --app <name> --addon <addon-id> backups              # List database backups
scalingo --app <name> --addon <addon-id> backups-download --backup <backup-id>
scalingo --app <name> --addon <addon-id> backups-create       # Manual backup
scalingo --app <name> --addon <addon-id> backups-config --schedule-at 3   # Daily backup hour
scalingo --app <name> --addon postgresql database-pitr-recovery-window   # Restorable time range
scalingo --app <name> --addon postgresql database-pitr-restore 2026-07-18T23:00:00Z   # PITR (RFC 3339 time)

Plans can be listed with scalingo database-list-plans. For Dedicated Resources databases (not attached to an app), use --database <database-id> instead of --app/--addon.

Domains and TLS

scalingo --app <name> domains                    # List
scalingo --app <name> domains-add example.com    # Add; Let's Encrypt cert auto-issued
scalingo --app <name> domains-remove example.com
scalingo --app <name> domains-ssl --cert cert.pem --key key.pem example.com   # Bring your own cert
scalingo --app <name> set-canonical-domain example.com   # Force redirects to this domain
scalingo --app <name> unset-canonical-domain

Let's Encrypt certificates are valid 45 days and renewed automatically. Every app has a default subdomain: <name>.osc-fr1.scalingo.io (or the equivalent for other regions). HTTPS is enabled by default and HTTP redirects to HTTPS automatically — disable via FORCE_HTTPS=false if needed.

Logs

scalingo --app <name> logs                       # Recent
scalingo --app <name> logs -f                    # Stream
scalingo --app <name> logs --lines 1000          # More history
scalingo --app <name> logs --filter worker       # Filter by process type
scalingo --app <name> logs-archives              # List archived log files
scalingo --app <name> logs-archives --page 2

Log drains (forward to external systems):

scalingo --app <name> log-drains                 # List drains
scalingo --app <name> log-drains --with-addons   # Include addon drains
scalingo --app <name> log-drains-add --type syslog --host <host> --port <port>
scalingo --app <name> log-drains-add --type=elk --url=https://user:pass@host/path
scalingo --app <name> log-drains-add --type=datadog --url=<datadog-url>
scalingo --app <name> log-drains-remove <drain-url>

# Addon logs drain (database addons only; separate from app logs)
scalingo --app <name> log-drains-add --addon <addon-id> --type syslog --host <host> --port <port>

Collaborators and access

scalingo --app <name> collaborators              # List
scalingo --app <name> collaborators-add email@example.com
scalingo --app <name> collaborators-remove email@example.com

Collaborators accept or decline by email. They can read/write to the app but can't destroy it unless granted ownership transfer. A Limited Collaborator role also exists for restricted access (set it in the dashboard).

SCM integrations and review apps

Link an app to a GitHub/GitLab repo for auto-deploy and review apps:

# Link the Scalingo user account to the SCM provider first (one-time, in dashboard → Account → Integrations)
# Then link a specific app to a specific repo:
scalingo --app <name> integration-link-create \
  --auto-deploy --branch main \
  https://github.com/org/repo

scalingo --app <name> integration-link           # Show current link
scalingo --app <name> integration-link-update --auto-deploy --branch develop
scalingo --app <name> integration-link-delete
scalingo --app <name> integration-link-manual-deploy main

# Review apps
scalingo --app <name> integration-link-update --deploy-review-apps --destroy-on-close
scalingo --app <name> integration-link-manual-review-app <pull-request-number>

Events and audit

scalingo --app <name> timeline       # Actions on this app
scalingo user-timeline               # Your actions across all apps

Stats and metrics

scalingo --app <name> stats          # Live CPU / RAM per container
scalingo --app <name> ps             # Container list with size and status

Router metrics (RPM, response times, 5xx) are visible in the dashboard and used by the autoscaler.

Addon configuration

Scalingo managed databases expose configurable features and users:

scalingo --app <name> --addon <addon-id> database-enable-feature force-ssl
scalingo --app <name> --addon <addon-id> database-disable-feature force-ssl
scalingo --app <name> --addon postgresql database-users-list
scalingo --app <name> --addon postgresql database-users-create --read-only <username>   # password prompted; blank = generated
scalingo --app <name> --addon postgresql database-users-update-password <username>
scalingo --app <name> --addon postgresql database-users-delete <username>

--addon accepts the addon ID or the addon type (e.g. postgresql) when the app has a single addon of that type. Features vary by engine — force-ssl (optional on every plan) and publicly-available are the common ones. PostgreSQL extensions such as pg_stat_statements are enabled with SQL (CREATE EXTENSION), not as features.

Firewall, output format, and preview features

# Application Firewall (launched 2026-10): restrict inbound traffic to an app
scalingo --app <name> app-firewall-rules
scalingo --app <name> app-firewall-rule-add --cidr 203.0.113.42/32 --label office
scalingo --app <name> app-firewall-rule-remove <rule-id>

# Machine-readable output (global flag; not every command supports it yet)
scalingo --format json --app <name> apps-info

# Preview commands (Dedicated Resources databases, database firewall rules, net peerings, ...)
export SCALINGO_PREVIEW_FEATURES=true
scalingo help

documents.label: Deployment on Scalingo
documents.html:
Deployment on Scalingo

Four deployment methods (there is no deploy-from-Docker-image option). Pick based on where your code lives and how much automation you want.

MethodWhen to useTrigger
Git pushLocal development, full controlgit push scalingo main
GitHub integrationTeam workflow, review apps per PRPush to linked branch
GitLab integrationSame as GitHub, GitLab-hosted reposPush to linked branch
ArchiveCI-built artifacts, no git history exposedscalingo deploy with a tarball path or URL
WARJVM apps with a prebuilt WARscalingo deploy --war

The deployment pipeline

Every method lands in the same pipeline:

  1. Ingest — source code or pre-built artifact arrives at Scalingo
  2. Build — a buildpack detects the stack, installs dependencies, produces a slug (compiled artifact)
  3. Postdeploy — if the Procfile has a postdeploy line, it runs once in a separate one-off container (size M, 20-minute limit) before traffic is switched (e.g. migrations)
  4. Swap — new containers start; routers wait for them to be healthy; old containers stop only once new ones serve traffic (zero-downtime)

There is no release process type on Scalingo — a Heroku release: line must become postdeploy:.

Limits: the build runs in a container with 6 CPUs and 8 GB of RAM, must finish within 30 minutes, and the resulting image can't exceed 2 GiB.

The build is cached between deploys — scalingo deployment-delete-cache forces a full rebuild.

Git push

Each app has its own git repo on Scalingo's side. Deploying is a push to the remote.

# Create the app
scalingo create my-app

# Get the remote URL (region-dependent)
scalingo --app my-app git-show
# → git@ssh.osc-fr1.scalingo.com:my-app.git

# Add the remote and push
git remote add scalingo git@ssh.osc-fr1.scalingo.com:my-app.git
git push scalingo main

Only master and main are accepted on the remote. To deploy a different local branch:

git push scalingo feature-x:main

To deploy a specific commit (not just HEAD):

git push scalingo <commit-sha>:main

To re-clone a Scalingo-hosted repo (e.g. after losing a local copy):

git clone --origin scalingo git@ssh.osc-fr1.scalingo.com:my-app.git

Only git-pushed code is in that repo — deploys made via GitHub integration, archive, or WAR don't populate it.

GitHub / GitHub Enterprise

Linking an app to GitHub enables:

  • Auto-deploy on push to a branch
  • Manual deploy from any branch
  • Review apps (ephemeral app per pull request)

Dashboard setup (recommended for the initial link)

  1. Account → Integrations → GitHub → Connect
  2. App → Deploy → Configuration → choose repo and branch
  3. Toggle Auto-deploy and/or Review apps

CLI setup

You need a GitHub personal access token with repo scope:

# Link your Scalingo user to GitHub
scalingo integrations-add github --token <github-pat>

# Link an app to a repo (creates the integration-link)
scalingo --app my-app integration-link-create \
  --auto-deploy --branch main \
  https://github.com/org/repo

# Subsequent updates
scalingo --app my-app integration-link-update --branch develop
scalingo --app my-app integration-link-update --no-auto-deploy

# Enable review apps (with destroy-on-close)
scalingo --app my-app integration-link-update \
  --deploy-review-apps --destroy-on-close

# Manual deploy (from a branch, bypassing auto-deploy)
scalingo --app my-app integration-link-manual-deploy main

GitHub Enterprise works identically with a custom host: replace github.com in the URL with your GHE host.

Fork review apps

Review apps from forked PRs are disabled by default — they inherit the parent app's environment, which would leak secrets to untrusted forks. Enable explicitly only if you trust the forks:

scalingo --app my-app integration-link-update --allow-review-apps-from-forks

A safer alternative: override sensitive env vars in scalingo.json so review apps don't inherit them.

GitLab

Works the same as GitHub — link a GitLab user account under Account → Integrations → GitLab, then:

scalingo --app my-app integration-link-create \
  --auto-deploy --branch main \
  https://gitlab.com/org/repo

Self-hosted GitLab instances work by passing the full URL to your instance.

Archive deploy

Deploy a .tar.gz of your source code, from a local file or a URL. Useful for CI pipelines that build artifacts independently.

Archive shape — code must live inside a single top-level folder (any name; master/ is just the usual example):

my-app.tar.gz
└── master/
    ├── package.json
    ├── Procfile
    └── src/...

One-liner to create such an archive from a git repo:

git archive --prefix=master/ main | gzip > my-app.tar.gz

Deploy from a local file or a URL:

scalingo --app my-app deploy my-app.tar.gz
scalingo --app my-app deploy https://example.com/my-app.tar.gz
# Optional second arg: a version reference (tag, commit SHA) for the deployment record
scalingo --app my-app deploy https://example.com/my-app.tar.gz v1.2.3
# Return immediately instead of following the build
scalingo --app my-app deploy --no-follow my-app.tar.gz v1.2.3

The URL must be reachable from Scalingo's build infrastructure (public, or behind auth encoded in the URL).

GitHub tarball shortcut

GitHub serves repo tarballs under a predictable URL:

scalingo --app my-app deploy \
  https://github.com/org/repo/archive/refs/heads/main.tar.gz

Useful for the one-click deploy button flow.

WAR

For JVM apps with a prebuilt WAR, the deploy command takes a --war flag:

scalingo --app my-app deploy --war ./target/app.war

There is no deploy-jar or deploy-war command, and no JAR upload: for JAR-based apps, deploy the source and let the Java buildpack build it. The Procfile still decides how web starts, typically:

web: java -jar target/app.jar

Auto-deploy workflow notes

  • Auto-deploy triggers on every push to the linked branch, not just the default branch
  • A failed build does not roll back — containers keep running the previous version
  • A failed postdeploy command (e.g. a migration) fails the deploy — the old containers keep serving
  • Review apps created from PRs get parent-app-name-pr<N> naming by default

One-click deploy buttons

A URL that deploys a scalingo.json-equipped public repo when clicked:

https://dashboard.scalingo.com/create/app?source=https://github.com/org/repo

With a custom branch:

https://dashboard.scalingo.com/create/app?source=https://github.com/org/repo#develop

Embed as a button in a README:

[![Deploy](https://cdn.scalingo.com/deploy/button.svg)](https://dashboard.scalingo.com/create/app?source=https://github.com/org/repo)

The scalingo.json manifest controls which addons and env vars the new app gets — see references/manifest-review-apps.md.

Build cache

Caches go per-app. Buildpacks decide what to cache (npm deps, wheel files, compiled binaries). When a deploy fails inexplicably after working previously, and a dependency is suspect, clear it:

scalingo --app my-app deployment-delete-cache

Next deploy will rebuild from scratch.

Troubleshooting common deployment errors

SymptomLikely causeFix
! [remote rejected] main -> main (pre-receive hook declined)You don't have admin on the appscalingo --app <n> collaborators to check
Push rejected, missing ProcfileNo Procfile and no default process type from buildpackAdd a Procfile
Detected buildpack: … wrongFramework-file present but minorSet BUILDPACK_URL env to force a specific buildpack
Build succeeds, app crashes at bootMissing env var or port bindingCheck logs, verify app binds to $PORT
Build runs old codeStale cachedeployment-delete-cache, redeploy
Review apps inherit prod credentialsNo scalingo.json env overridesAdd env block to scalingo.json

documents.label: scalingo.json Manifest and Review Apps
documents.html:
scalingo.json Manifest and Review Apps

scalingo.json is the app manifest — a declarative file describing how an app should be configured when created from a one-click deploy button or as a review app. It's the Scalingo equivalent of Heroku's app.json, and the shapes are near-identical for common fields.

Important scope: the manifest is evaluated only when an app is created via one-click deploy or as a review app. It is not re-read on later deploys of that app, nor on ordinary git push deploys. Production addons, env vars, and formation are managed via the CLI/dashboard/Terraform after the initial creation.

File location

At repo root, named scalingo.json. If both scalingo.json and app.json exist, scalingo.json wins.

If your code lives in a subdirectory (configured via the PROJECT_DIR env var), place the manifest in that subdirectory.

Full example

{
  "name": "Sample App",
  "description": "Example service illustrating the manifest",
  "logo": "https://example.com/logo.svg",
  "repository": "https://github.com/org/repo",
  "website": "https://example.com",
  "stack": "scalingo-26",
  "env": {
    "ENVIRONMENT": {
      "description": "Runtime environment identifier",
      "value": "staging"
    },
    "SECRET_KEY": {
      "description": "App secret for signing sessions",
      "generator": "secret"
    },
    "PUBLIC_URL": {
      "description": "URL of the deployed app",
      "generator": "url"
    },
    "ADMIN_URL": {
      "description": "Admin panel URL",
      "generator": "url",
      "template": "%URL%/admin"
    }
  },
  "formation": {
    "web":    { "amount": 2, "size": "L" },
    "worker": { "amount": 1, "size": "M" }
  },
  "addons": [
    {
      "plan": "postgresql:postgresql-starter-512",
      "options": { "version": "17" }
    },
    {
      "plan": "redis:redis-starter-256"
    }
  ],
  "scripts": {
    "first-deploy": "bundle exec rake db:migrate db:seed"
  }
}

Field reference

Top-level metadata

FieldTypeNotes
namestringDisplay name in the deploy page
descriptionstringShown to the user before they confirm
logoURLRendered on the deploy page
repositoryURLSource repo (used if URL param isn't provided)
websiteURLProject homepage
stackstringStack for the new app (scalingo-26 is the default; scalingo-22 is deprecated) — usually omit to let the platform pick
firewall_rulesarrayApplication Firewall rules to create with the app (see the official manifest docs for the exact shape)

env

Keys are env var names. Values are objects describing how the variable is sourced:

  • value (string) — hardcoded default
  • description (string) — shown in the UI
  • required (bool) — if true, user must supply a value
  • generator — one of secret (random 64-char hex string), url (the app's Scalingo URL)
  • template (string, with generator: url) — transform the URL; %URL% is the placeholder

Review apps: if a variable is listed in the manifest's env, it's populated from the generator/value rather than inherited from the parent app. This is the primary mechanism for preventing review apps from picking up production credentials.

formation

A map of process type → { amount, size }. Applied at creation time. Ordinary process types (web, worker, ...) are valid; size defaults to M if omitted.

addons

Array of objects. Each addon is specified as "<provider>:<plan>". Optional options.version pins an engine version (e.g. PostgreSQL "17"). Sandbox plans no longer exist; use the smallest Starter plan.

Common plan identifiers:

  • postgresql:postgresql-starter-512, postgresql:postgresql-business-1024
  • mysql:mysql-starter-512
  • mongodb:mongo-starter-512 (smallest is 256 MB)
  • redis:redis-starter-256 (smallest Caching plan)
  • opensearch:opensearch-starter-1024 (smallest OpenSearch plan)

Validate with scalingo addons-list and scalingo addons-plans <provider>.

scripts

  • first-deploy (preferred) — runs once, after the first deployment of a review app or one-click app completes. Retried until it succeeds. Use for initial migrations and seed data.
  • postdeploy (deprecated at manifest level; use postdeploy in the Procfile instead) — runs after every deployment of a review app except the first if first-deploy is defined.

For production apps, move postdeploy into the Procfile:

postdeploy: bundle exec rake db:migrate

This runs for every deploy of every linked app (parent + review apps). If you need review-app-only behavior, guard with an env var:

{
  "env": { "IS_REVIEW_APP": { "value": "true" } }
}

Then in your script check IS_REVIEW_APP.

Review apps

Review apps are ephemeral apps spawned from pull requests on a linked SCM. Enable on the parent app:

scalingo --app parent-app integration-link-update \
  --deploy-review-apps --destroy-on-close

A review app's default configuration:

  • Name: <parent>-pr<N> (plus a hash for uniqueness)
  • Env: parent's env minus any keys overridden in scalingo.json
  • Addons: provisioned fresh per manifest; parent addons are not copied (data starts empty)
  • Formation: from manifest, or 1 × M web default
  • Collaborators: inherited from parent

Lifecycle

  • Created: when the PR is opened (auto) or manually via CLI
  • Redeployed: on every push to the PR branch (auto-deploy)
  • Destroyed: when the PR is closed (--destroy-on-close) or after a period of inactivity (--destroy-on-stale with --hours-before-destroy-on-stale)

Manually creating a review app

scalingo --app parent-app integration-link-manual-review-app <pr-number>

Configuration flags

scalingo --app parent-app integration-link-update \
  --deploy-review-apps \
  --destroy-on-close \
  --hours-before-destroy-on-close 2 \
  --destroy-on-stale \
  --hours-before-destroy-on-stale 168 \
  --allow-review-apps-from-forks    # see security note below

Fork safety

By default, PRs from forks do not spawn review apps — they would inherit the parent's env, which means secrets. Enable forks only if you trust the fork authors (rarely the case for public repos). A safer middle ground: use scalingo.json's env to override every sensitive key with a generator, then enable fork PRs.

Protecting review apps with basic auth

Review apps are publicly reachable by default. To gate them:

{
  "env": {
    "HTTP_BASIC_AUTH_USER": { "value": "reviewer" },
    "HTTP_BASIC_AUTH_PASS": { "generator": "secret" }
  }
}

Your app code reads these vars and conditionally applies basic auth middleware. The presence of HTTP_BASIC_AUTH_PASS (generator returns a random secret per review app) is what distinguishes a review app from production, where the var is absent.

Per-review-app behavior flag

Common pattern to branch app behavior:

{
  "env": {
    "IS_REVIEW_APP": { "value": "true" }
  }
}

Production doesn't define IS_REVIEW_APP, review apps do. Use in your code:

if os.environ.get("IS_REVIEW_APP"):
    # skip outbound webhooks to third parties
    # seed test data instead of pulling from prod S3

One-click deploy button

The manifest powers the one-click deploy flow. Button URL:

https://dashboard.scalingo.com/create/app?source=https://github.com/org/repo

With a specific branch:

https://dashboard.scalingo.com/create/app?source=https://github.com/org/repo#develop

Embed in a README:

[![Deploy on Scalingo](https://cdn.scalingo.com/deploy/button.svg)](https://dashboard.scalingo.com/create/app?source=https://github.com/org/repo)

The button takes the user to a page that shows the manifest's name, description, env prompts, and addons. They pick a name and region, then the platform provisions everything and deploys.

Only public GitHub repos are supported for one-click deploy.

Common patterns

Generating a per-app secret

{
  "env": {
    "JWT_SECRET": { "generator": "secret" }
  }
}

A different 64-char hex string per review app. Never commit secrets.

Per-app canonical URL

{
  "env": {
    "CANONICAL_HOST_URL": { "generator": "url" }
  }
}

CANONICAL_HOST_URL receives the review app's own URL (e.g. https://my-app-pr42-abc.osc-fr1.scalingo.io), useful for callback URLs and OAuth redirects.

Skipping addons on review apps

If review apps don't need a full Business-tier database, override the manifest to request a Starter plan only in review apps. The manifest drives review-app addons, so it's already the simpler plan unless you explicitly set Business. Keep production addons on the Business plan via CLI/Terraform.

Scoping a postdeploy to review apps only

In scalingo.json:

{
  "env": { "RUN_TEST_SEED": { "value": "1" } },
  "scripts": { "first-deploy": "bundle exec rake db:migrate db:seed" }
}

In the Procfile:

postdeploy: [ -z "$RUN_TEST_SEED" ] && bundle exec rake db:migrate || true

Production apps (no RUN_TEST_SEED) run only db:migrate. Review apps get the seeded dataset via first-deploy once at creation.

documents.label: Scaling and Autoscaler
documents.html:
Scaling and Autoscaler

Two orthogonal dimensions of scaling, plus an automated controller for horizontal scaling.

Horizontal scaling

Add or remove containers of a given process type. Traffic is load-balanced across all running containers for that type.

scalingo --app my-app scale web:5:M      # 5 web containers of size M
scalingo --app my-app scale worker:3     # 3 workers (size unchanged)

Benefits:

  • Fault tolerance — one container failure doesn't take the service down
  • Near-infinite headroom — add containers as traffic grows
  • Cost control — combined with autoscaling, you pay for peak capacity only when you need it

Good for stateless web servers, job workers, and anything designed for distributed workloads.

Vertical scaling

Change the container size (memory and CPU priority).

scalingo --app my-app scale web:2:XL     # 2 containers, upgrade to XL

Container tiers:

SizeMemoryCPU priorityPID limit
S256 MBlow128
M512 MBstandard256
L1 GBstandard512
XL2 GBhigh1024
2XL4 GBhigh2048
3XL8 GBhigh—

XL and larger receive roughly double the CPU priority of M/L in contested situations. 3XL is the largest size and has been self-service since 2026-07-21; there is no 4XL or 8XL. A process type can run up to 10 containers by default (ask support for more).

Swap is going away. It was removed for new customers from 2026-06-01 and new apps from 2026-09-01, and it will be removed from all containers on 2027-01-01. An app that relies on swap today may be OOM-killed once it is gone, so pick a size whose RAM covers the real peak.

Vertical scaling suits:

  • Legacy apps not designed for distribution
  • Memory-hungry runtimes (JVM, Rails, Meteor)
  • Predictable workloads where the cost of coordination outweighs the benefit of distribution

The two are complementary — most production apps combine both (e.g. 3 × L web containers).

Scaling semantics

  • Scaling up/down/out/in is zero-downtime — new containers start and pass health checks before old ones are stopped
  • Starting a process type from 0 triggers a cold start (image pull, app boot)
  • Stopping is fast — running containers are sent SIGTERM, have a grace period, then SIGKILL
  • If an autoscaler is active on a process type, disable it (autoscalers-disable <type>) before scaling that type by hand, so the two don't conflict

The Scalingo Autoscaler

Built-in horizontal autoscaler. Configure per process type, based on a target metric.

Enable via dashboard

App → Resources → select process type → Autoscale → pick metric, target, min, max.

Enable via CLI

Autoscalers are identified by container type, not by an ID. All five flags are required on autoscalers-add.

scalingo --app my-app autoscalers-add --container-type web \
  --metric cpu --target 0.75 --min-containers 2 --max-containers 10

scalingo --app my-app autoscalers                  # list
scalingo --app my-app autoscalers-update --container-type web --target 0.6
scalingo --app my-app autoscalers-update -c web --disabled   # or autoscalers-disable web
scalingo --app my-app autoscalers-disable web
scalingo --app my-app autoscalers-enable web
scalingo --app my-app autoscalers-remove web

Short flags: -c (container type), -m (metric), -t (target). cpu targets are ratios (0.75 = 75%), not percentages; check the dashboard's suggested value for the other metrics. The minimum is 2 containers, so a single-container app can't be autoscaled.

Available metrics

MetricWhat it measuresBest forAggregation
cpuCPU % per containerGeneral-purpose web appsMean across containers
memoryRAM usage per containerMemory-bound appsMean across containers
swapSwap usage %Leak detection / oversized workloadMean
rpm_per_containerRequests per minute / containerTraffic-driven scalingSum / n
p95_response_timep95 response timeUser-experience-driven scalingp95 across requests
5XXServer errors per minuteReliability-driven scalingSum per minute

Recommended targets for router-based metrics (RPM, response time, 5xx) are computed from your app's own last-24h median — Scalingo surfaces these in the dashboard as starting points.

Finding the right target: scale down to 1 container (with the autoscaler disabled), run a load test (Locust, k6, Artillery), and find the saturation point. Set the target 20–30% below saturation so the autoscaler has time to add capacity.

Scaling rules

The autoscaler follows conservative rules to avoid thrashing:

  • Cooldown after scale-out: 1 minute — no second scale-out allowed in that window
  • Cooldown after scale-in: 3 minutes — cautious about removing capacity
  • Step: normally 1 container per decision round. The exception is rpm_per_container, where the autoscaler can add multiple containers per round if traffic spikes steeply (still capped at your max)
  • Min/max respected: hard floor and ceiling

Effective for moderate ramp-up and ramp-down. Not designed for sudden 10× spikes — for predictable traffic events (product launches, news mentions), manually scale up beforehand.

Response time caveat

A rising p95 response time doesn't always mean the containers are saturated. It may reflect:

  • Slow database queries
  • External API latency
  • GC pressure inside the runtime

Don't set p95_response_time-based autoscaling without first confirming it's container saturation, not a downstream bottleneck. The autoscaler can't fix a slow database by adding web containers.

5xx caveat

5XX triggers scaling on server error rate per minute. This only helps if errors are caused by overload (502/504 from request-queue overflow). Errors from bugs or bad config will cause the autoscaler to add capacity without fixing anything.

Request queueing and router behavior

Understanding these numbers makes autoscaler targets saner:

  • Each router keeps a local request queue per app
  • Queue size: 50 requests per web container
  • Once full, new requests get 503 Service Unavailable
  • Example: 2 × web containers → 100 queued requests max

Queue-full = you're undersized. Either scale or optimize response time. RPM-based autoscaling is the right tool for predictable traffic growth; response-time-based is the right tool for unpredictable slowness.

Scaling via Terraform

resource "scalingo_container_type" "web" {
  app    = scalingo_app.my_app.name
  name   = "web"
  amount = 2
  size   = "L"
}

resource "scalingo_container_type" "worker" {
  app    = scalingo_app.my_app.name
  name   = "worker"
  amount = 1
  size   = "M"
}

terraform apply is the scale operation. Manual CLI scales outside of Terraform will drift — either don't mix, or use terraform refresh followed by config updates.

When to scale what

Quick decision guide:

  • High RAM, low CPU → vertical scale up (bigger container)
  • High CPU, moderate RAM → horizontal scale out (more containers)
  • Bursty traffic, predictable patterns → autoscaler with RPM target
  • Bursty traffic, unpredictable → autoscaler with response-time target, plus slightly higher min
  • Steady state, no budget flexibility → manual scaling to a fixed formation, no autoscaler
  • Background job worker accumulating backlog → horizontal scale out (more workers); autoscale on queue length is not a built-in metric, so scale manually from worker-side signals or a custom script via the API

documents.label: Scalingo Terraform Provider
documents.html:
Scalingo Terraform Provider

The official Scalingo Terraform provider (v2.8.0 as of 2026-09) manages apps (and their environment), addons, container types, autoscalers, alerts, domains, SCM integrations, collaborators, log drains, projects, firewall rules, SSH keys, and Dedicated Resources databases declaratively.

  • Provider: Scalingo/scalingo
  • Registry: https://registry.terraform.io/providers/Scalingo/scalingo/latest/docs
  • Opinionated module: scalingo-community/app/scalingo (wraps common patterns)

Setup

terraform {
  required_providers {
    scalingo = {
      source  = "Scalingo/scalingo"
      version = "~> 2.0"   # use "~> 2.8" for scalingo_app_firewall_rule
    }
  }
}

provider "scalingo" {
  region = "osc-fr1"
  # api_token is picked up from SCALINGO_API_TOKEN env var
}

Authentication — prefer env vars over hardcoded tokens:

export SCALINGO_API_TOKEN="tk-us-..."
export SCALINGO_REGION="osc-fr1"     # or osc-secnum-fr1

Generate the token in the Scalingo dashboard: Account Settings → API Tokens.

Never commit a token into Terraform files that hit version control.

Core resources

scalingo_app

data "scalingo_stack" "s26" {
  name = "scalingo-26"
}

resource "scalingo_app" "api" {
  name        = "my-api"
  stack_id    = data.scalingo_stack.s26.id   # optional; the attribute is stack_id, not stack
  project_id  = scalingo_project.main.id   # optional
  force_https = true
  environment = {
    DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE = "myapp.settings.prod"
    LOG_LEVEL              = "INFO"
  }
}

The provider's example resolves the stack through the scalingo_stack data source; Scalingo's own tutorials pass the slug directly (stack_id = "scalingo-26"). Other optional attributes: router_logs, sticky_session, hds_resource. all_environment is a read-only map that also includes addon-injected variables.

Outputs useful later: scalingo_app.api.name, scalingo_app.api.id, scalingo_app.api.url (the default subdomain URL), scalingo_app.api.git_url.

scalingo_addon

resource "scalingo_addon" "db" {
  provider_id = "postgresql"
  plan        = "postgresql-starter-512"
  app         = scalingo_app.api.id

  database_features = ["force-ssl"]   # optional toggles
}

The addon block is where you set up managed databases. List provider IDs with scalingo addons-list (or the scalingo_addon_providers data source) and plans with scalingo addons-plans <provider>. The provider's own example uses scalingo-redis with redis-starter-256. Import format: <app-id>:<addon-id>.

scalingo_container_type — formation

One resource per process type:

resource "scalingo_container_type" "web" {
  app    = scalingo_app.api.name
  name   = "web"
  amount = 2
  size   = "L"
}

resource "scalingo_container_type" "worker" {
  app    = scalingo_app.api.name
  name   = "worker"
  amount = 1
  size   = "M"
}

Manual CLI scaling will drift from Terraform state — either manage scaling exclusively via Terraform (and commit changes) or not at all. Mixing leads to confusion.

scalingo_domain

resource "scalingo_domain" "apex" {
  common_name = "example.com"
  app         = scalingo_app.api.id
}

Let's Encrypt cert is auto-issued once DNS points to Scalingo. The resource only supports common_name, app, canonical (redirect all traffic to this domain, one per app), and letsencrypt_enabled (default true):

resource "scalingo_domain" "www" {
  common_name = "www.example.com"
  app         = scalingo_app.api.id
  canonical   = true
}

There are no tls_cert / tls_key attributes. To use a custom certificate, set letsencrypt_enabled = false and upload the certificate outside Terraform: scalingo --app my-api domains-ssl --cert cert.pem --key key.pem secure.example.com.

scalingo_collaborator

resource "scalingo_collaborator" "teammate" {
  app     = scalingo_app.api.id
  email   = "teammate@example.com"
  limited = false   # true = Limited Collaborator role
}

The person receives an email invite. Terraform doesn't wait for acceptance.

scalingo_scm_integration and scalingo_scm_repo_link

GitHub.com and GitLab.com integrations are created once from the dashboard and read with a data source. The scalingo_scm_integration resource is only for github-enterprise and gitlab-self-hosted.

data "scalingo_scm_integration" "github" {
  scm_type = "github"
}

resource "scalingo_scm_repo_link" "api_repo" {
  source                       = "https://github.com/org/api-repo"
  branch                       = "main"
  auth_integration_uuid        = data.scalingo_scm_integration.github.id
  app                          = scalingo_app.api.id
  auto_deploy_enabled          = true
  deploy_review_apps_enabled   = true
  delete_on_close_enabled      = true
  hours_before_delete_on_close = 2
  delete_stale_enabled         = true
  hours_before_delete_stale    = 168
}

# Self-hosted SCM only
resource "scalingo_scm_integration" "gitlab_internal" {
  scm_type     = "gitlab-self-hosted"
  url          = "https://gitlab.example.com"
  access_token = var.gitlab_token
}

This replaces the one-off CLI setup with reproducible config.

scalingo_log_drain

resource "scalingo_log_drain" "syslog" {
  app  = scalingo_app.api.id
  type = "syslog"
  host = "logs.example.com"
  port = "6514"
}

# Addon (database) log drain: same resource, with the addon UUID
resource "scalingo_log_drain" "db_syslog" {
  app   = scalingo_app.api.id
  addon = scalingo_addon.db.id
  type  = "syslog"
  host  = "logs.example.com"
  port  = "6514"
}

url is a sensitive helper that fills host/port/token; token and drain_region are used by some vendors. There is no scalingo_log_drain_addon resource.

scalingo_notifier and notification platforms

For alerting integrations (Slack, email, webhook). Look up the platform with the scalingo_notification_platform data source, then create notifiers and scalingo_alert resources that reference them:

data "scalingo_notification_platform" "email" {
  name = "email"
}

resource "scalingo_notifier" "ops" {
  app         = scalingo_app.api.id
  platform_id = data.scalingo_notification_platform.email.id
  name        = "Ops email"
  emails      = ["ops@example.com"]
}

resource "scalingo_alert" "web_cpu" {
  app            = scalingo_app.api.id
  container_type = "web"
  metric         = "cpu"
  limit          = 0.8
  notifiers      = [scalingo_notifier.ops.id]
}

scalingo_autoscaler

resource "scalingo_autoscaler" "web_rpm" {
  app            = scalingo_app.api.id
  container_type = "web"
  metric         = "rpm_per_container"
  target         = 200
  min_containers = 2   # the autoscaler needs at least 2
  max_containers = 10
}

Metric names match the CLI (cpu, memory, swap, rpm_per_container, p95_response_time, 5XX); cpu targets are ratios (0.8 = 80%). Set disabled = true to pause without deleting. Import format: <app-id>:<autoscaler-id>.

Managing autoscalers via Terraform is the cleanest approach for production — the formation block sets initial capacity, the autoscaler adjusts from there.

Environment variables

There is no scalingo_env_var resource. Env vars live in the environment map of scalingo_app:

locals {
  app_env = {
    DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE = "myapp.settings.prod"
    SENTRY_DSN             = var.sentry_dsn
    LOG_LEVEL              = "INFO"
  }
}

resource "scalingo_app" "api" {
  name        = "my-api"
  environment = local.app_env
}

Variables injected by addons (e.g. SCALINGO_POSTGRESQL_URL) don't belong in this map; read them from scalingo_app.api.all_environment if needed.

Remember: env changes via Terraform don't trigger a restart. Pair with a null_resource calling scalingo restart on changes, or restart manually:

resource "null_resource" "restart_on_env_change" {
  triggers = {
    env_hash = md5(jsonencode(local.app_env))
  }

  provisioner "local-exec" {
    command = "scalingo --app ${scalingo_app.api.name} restart"
  }
}

Projects, firewall rules, and Dedicated Resources databases

resource "scalingo_project" "main" {
  name    = "payments"
  default = false
}

# Application Firewall: restrict inbound traffic to listed IPv4 CIDRs (provider >= 2.8)
resource "scalingo_app_firewall_rule" "office" {
  app   = scalingo_app.api.id
  cidr  = "192.0.2.0/24"
  label = "office"
}

# Dedicated Resources PostgreSQL (preview), not attached to an app
resource "scalingo_database" "pg" {
  name       = "my-postgres-db"
  technology = "postgresql-ng"
  plan       = "postgresql-ng-enterprise-4096"
  project_id = scalingo_project.main.id
}

resource "scalingo_database_firewall_rule" "office" {
  database_id = scalingo_database.pg.database_id
  cidr        = "203.0.113.0/24"
  label       = "Office network"
}

Also available: scalingo_ssh_key, and data sources such as scalingo_stack, scalingo_region, scalingo_container_size, scalingo_project, scalingo_private_network_domain, and scalingo_database_endpoints (provider >= 2.8).

Importing existing resources

Existing apps and addons can be imported into Terraform state:

# App (import by name or ID)
terraform import scalingo_app.api my-api

# Addon (format: <app-id>:<addon-id>)
terraform import scalingo_addon.db <app-id>:ad-xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx

# Domain (format: <app-id>:<domain-id>, the domain's ID, not its hostname)
terraform import scalingo_domain.www <app-id>:<domain-id>

# Autoscaler (format: <app-id>:<autoscaler-id>)
terraform import scalingo_autoscaler.web <app-id>:<autoscaler-id>

Env vars are imported with the app (they are part of its environment map).

After import, run terraform plan and reconcile any drift.

The opinionated community module

scalingo-community/app/scalingo bundles an app with its database, env, formation, log drains, and review-app config in one module call:

module "api" {
  source  = "scalingo-community/app/scalingo"
  version = "~> 0.6"   # v0.6.0 needs provider ~> 2.7; default stack scalingo-26

  name   = "my-api"
  domain = "api.example.com"

  environment = {
    LOG_LEVEL = "INFO"
  }

  containers = {
    web    = { size = "L", amount = 2 }
    worker = { size = "M", amount = 1 }
  }

  addons = [
    { provider = "postgresql", plan = "postgresql-starter-512" },
    { provider = "redis",      plan = "redis-starter-256" },
  ]

  log_drains = [
    { type = "elk", url = "https://user:pass@logstash.example.com" }
  ]

  review_apps = {
    enabled                         = true
    delete_on_close_enabled         = true
    hours_before_delete_on_close    = "2"
    delete_stale_enabled            = true
    hours_before_delete_stale       = "168"
    automatic_creation_from_forks_allowed = false
  }
}

The module handles the resource wiring. Good for teams standardizing a fleet of similar apps.

State and secrets

  • Terraform state includes secret values (env vars, API tokens, log drain tokens). Store state remotely with encryption — S3+KMS, Terraform Cloud, or GitLab's managed backend.
  • Never commit .tfstate to git.
  • Use sensitive = true on outputs that include secrets.
  • For secrets sourced from a vault (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager), use the relevant data source to avoid duplicating secrets into tfvars files.

Multi-region setups

Target multiple regions in one Terraform run with provider aliases:

provider "scalingo" {
  alias  = "fr1"
  region = "osc-fr1"
}

provider "scalingo" {
  alias  = "secnum"
  region = "osc-secnum-fr1"
}

resource "scalingo_app" "public" {
  provider = scalingo.fr1
  name     = "public-api"
}

resource "scalingo_app" "sovereign" {
  provider = scalingo.secnum
  name     = "sovereign-api"
}

Useful when a product spans both general and sovereign deployments.

CI/CD patterns

Typical GitHub Actions flow:

  1. CI builds and tests
  2. CI runs terraform plan (on PRs) and terraform apply (on merges to main)
  3. scalingo deploy (or git push) triggers the actual code deployment
  4. Terraform manages infra; git push/SCM integration manages code

Keep infra and app deployments as separate pipeline stages — Terraform changes shouldn't gate code pushes, and vice versa.

documents.label: Deployment Recipes from the Scalingo Tutorials Hub
documents.html:
Deployment Recipes from the Scalingo Tutorials Hub

Condensed, Scalingo-specific steps from the official Tutorials Hub (checked October 2026). Use these as starting points when a user wants to deploy a well-known tool. Always re-read the linked page before a real deployment: versions, env vars, and sample repos move.

Table of contents

  1. Status labels
  2. Patterns shared by the tutorials
  3. Keycloak (Projects + Private Networks)
  4. PostgREST with Keycloak JWT
  5. ModSecurity WAF on the nginx buildpack
  6. WordPress (Bedrock)
  7. n8n
  8. Metabase
  9. Judoscale autoscaling
  10. Lovable projects
  11. AI demos: Whisper, pgvector, OpenSearch RAG
  12. Elastic Stack (legacy)

Status labels

Each tutorial carries a label. It matters when you recommend one for production:

LabelMeaningPages
TutorialValidated by ScalingoKeycloak, ModSecurity, WordPress, n8n, Metabase
DemoNot a supported product; no guarantee it keeps working or suits productionPostgREST, Whisper, pgvector, Lovable, OpenSearch RAG, Elastic Stack
Demo / PartnerThird-party service with its own billingJudoscale

Patterns shared by the tutorials

  • Sample repo + push. Most tutorials clone a github.com/Scalingo/<tool>-scalingo repo, scalingo create, add an addon, and git push scalingo master (main works too).
  • Terraform variant. Several pages also show Terraform: scalingo_app (force_https = true), scalingo_scm_repo_link on the fork, scalingo_addon, scalingo_container_type, then terraform apply and a manual deployment from the dashboard (Deploy tab → Manual deployment), since creating the link does not deploy. Some older pages pin stack_id = "scalingo-22"; use scalingo-26 for new apps (see buildpacks.md).
  • Reference another env var without expanding it locally. Escape the $ so the value stays a reference that is resolved at runtime:
  scalingo --app my-app env-set PGRST_SERVER_PORT=\$PORT PGRST_DB_URI=\$SCALINGO_POSTGRESQL_URL
  • No local persistence. The filesystem is ephemeral, so tools that default to SQLite or local uploads need a database addon or object storage (n8n → PostgreSQL, WordPress media → S3).
  • Pin versions with env vars. Buildpacks for packaged tools install the latest tested version on every deploy unless you pin it (KEYCLOAK_VERSION, METABASE_VERSION, MODSECURITY_VERSION, ...). An empty commit plus a push is the usual way to upgrade:
  git commit --allow-empty -m "Upgrade" && git push scalingo master

Keycloak (Projects + Private Networks)

— clustered Keycloak (Infinispan cache) on a Private Network, published through an nginx reverse proxy. Sample repo: . 
scalingo projects-add keycloak
scalingo projects                                   # note the prj-... ID and the private network
scalingo create my-keycloak --project-id <project_id>
scalingo --app my-keycloak addons-add postgresql postgresql-business-1024
scalingo --app my-keycloak env-set BUILDPACK_URL=https://github.com/Scalingo/keycloak-buildpack
scalingo --app my-keycloak scale kc:3:XL
git push scalingo master

# Public reverse proxy in the same project
scalingo create my-nginx --project-id <project_id>
scalingo --app my-nginx env-set KEYCLOAK_PRIVATE_DOMAIN=kc.<private_network_fqdn>
kc: /app/keycloak/bin/kc.sh start --optimized
  • The process type is kc, not web, so Keycloak is not publicly exposed; only the nginx app is. nginx resolves the private domain with resolvers 10.255.0.10 10.255.0.11 and proxies only /realms/, /resources/, /.well-known/.
  • Mandatory env: KC_PROXY_HEADERS=xforwarded, KC_HTTP_ENABLED=true, KC_HTTP_PORT=8080, KC_HOSTNAME, KC_CACHE_EMBEDDED_NETWORK_BIND_ADDRESS="match-address:10.240.*" (cache traffic on the private network), KC_CACHE_STACK=jdbc-ping, KC_CACHE_CONFIG_MUTATE=true, KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_USERNAME, KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD. Recommended: KEYCLOAK_VERSION, KC_PROXY_TRUSTED_ADDRESSES.
  • Size: at least XL (about 1.5 GB RAM, CPU-heavy); a Business database for redundancy. Health/metrics endpoints are off by default (KC_HEALTH_ENABLED, KC_METRICS_ENABLED, management port 9000).
  • Back up the database before upgrading: Keycloak upgrades can migrate the schema.

PostgREST with Keycloak JWT

(Demo) — PostgreSQL as a REST API with JWT auth and Row-Level Security. 
scalingo create my-postgrest
scalingo --app my-postgrest addons-add postgresql postgresql-starter-512
scalingo --app my-postgrest env-set BUILDPACK_URL=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Scalingo/scalingo-labs/main/postgrest-buildpack/postgrest-buildpack.tar.gz
scalingo --app my-postgrest env-set POSTGREST_VERSION=<version>
scalingo --app my-postgrest env-set PGRST_DB_URI=\$SCALINGO_POSTGRESQL_URL PGRST_DB_SCHEMAS=api PGRST_SERVER_PORT=\$PORT
scalingo --app my-postgrest pgsql-console          # create schemas, roles, RLS policies
scalingo --app my-postgrest env-set PGRST_JWT_SECRET="$KEYCLOAK_JWKS" PGRST_JWT_AUD=postgrest-api
git commit --allow-empty -m "Deploy PostgREST" && git push scalingo main
  • PGRST_JWT_SECRET holds the Keycloak JWKS from <keycloak>/realms/<realm>/protocol/openid-connect/certs.
  • Use FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY: the PostgREST role owns the tables, and owners bypass plain RLS.
  • An M container is enough (PostgREST needs about 100–400 MB).

ModSecurity WAF on the nginx buildpack

— OWASP Core Rule Set in front of an app served by Scalingo's nginx buildpack. 
scalingo --app my-app env-set ENABLE_MODSECURITY=true
git commit --allow-empty -m "Enable ModSecurity" && git push scalingo master
curl -v -X INVALID_HTTP_METHOD https://my-app.osc-fr1.scalingo.io   # expect 403

Custom rules live in a repo file referenced from a location block of nginx.conf / nginx.conf.erb. The path must start with /app/:

modsecurity on;
modsecurity_rules_file /app/my_rules.conf;
  • Disable a rule with SecRuleRemoveById <id> at the end of the rules file.
  • Every deploy installs the latest ModSecurity and the latest LTS CRS. Pin MODSECURITY_VERSION and MODSECURITY_CORE_RULE_SET_VERSION to avoid surprise upgrades.
  • Logging: MODSECURITY_DEBUG_LOG_LEVEL (0–9), MODSECURITY_AUDIT_LOG_LEVEL (On / RelevantOnly / Off).
  • For IP allowlisting rather than request filtering, use the platform's Application Firewall (app-firewall-rule-add, see cli-reference.md).

WordPress (Bedrock)

— Bedrock-based WordPress on the PHP buildpack. Sample repo: . 
git clone https://github.com/Scalingo/wordpress-scalingo && cd wordpress-scalingo
scalingo create my-wordpress
scalingo --app my-wordpress addons-add mysql mysql-starter-512
scalingo --app my-wordpress scale web:1:XL          # optional
git push scalingo master                            # build log: "Detected Bedrock WordPress"
  • Mandatory env: WP_HOME (app URL), WP_SITEURL (app URL + /wp), and the eight keys/salts (AUTH_KEY, SECURE_AUTH_KEY, LOGGED_IN_KEY, NONCE_KEY, AUTH_SALT, SECURE_AUTH_SALT, LOGGED_IN_SALT, NONCE_SALT). WP_ENV defaults to production.
  • Media must go to object storage: local uploads are lost on restart. The repo bundles humanmade/s3-uploads; set S3_UPLOADS_BUCKET, S3_UPLOADS_KEY, S3_UPLOADS_SECRET, S3_UPLOADS_REGION (and optionally S3_UPLOADS_OBJECT_ACL). Any S3-compatible storage works.
  • Plugins: composer require --ignore-platform-reqs wpackagist-plugin/<name>, commit composer.json and composer.lock. Themes go in web/app/themes. Admin is at /wp/wp-admin.

n8n

— workflow automation. Sample repo: (Node.js app depending on the `n8n` package). 
git clone https://github.com/Scalingo/n8n-scalingo && cd n8n-scalingo
scalingo create my-n8n
scalingo --app my-n8n addons-add postgresql postgresql-starter-512
scalingo --app my-n8n scale web:1:XL
scalingo --app my-n8n env-set N8N_PORT=\$PORT N8N_PROTOCOL=https DB_TYPE=postgresdb N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY=<random-string>
git push scalingo master
  • SQLite (n8n's default) is not usable on Scalingo; PostgreSQL is required.
  • Start with XL: n8n is RAM-hungry. Scalingo's own production setup runs queue mode with multi-main: 2 × 2XL web, 2 × 2XL worker, PostgreSQL Business 2G, Caching Business 1G.
  • Upgrade: npm install n8n@<version> --package-lock-only, commit package.json and package-lock.json, push.

Metabase

— BI dashboards. Sample repo: . 
git clone https://github.com/Scalingo/metabase-scalingo && cd metabase-scalingo
scalingo create my-metabase
scalingo --app my-metabase addons-add postgresql postgresql-starter-512   # Metabase's own metadata DB
scalingo --app my-metabase scale web:1:XL
git push scalingo master
  • No mandatory env vars. Pin with METABASE_VERSION (must start with v); otherwise each deploy installs the latest.
  • Point Metabase at a copy of the production database rather than the live one, so analytics queries don't slow the app.

Judoscale autoscaling

(Partner) — autoscale on request or job **queue time** instead of the built-in metrics.
  1. Create a Scalingo API token (dashboard → Account → Tokens) and paste it in Judoscale; pick the project and app. The token carries all of its account's rights, so consider a dedicated account.
  2. Add the adapter package (Rails example: judoscale-rails, judoscale-sidekiq).
  3. scalingo --app my-app env-set JUDOSCALE_URL=<url from Judoscale> (treat it as a secret), commit, push.
  4. Disable the built-in Scalingo Autoscaler on that process type first (autoscalers-disable web): one autoscaler per process type.

Min/max container counts are set in Judoscale; the max is your cost ceiling. Works for web (request queue) and workers (job queue).

Lovable projects

(Demo) — deploy a Lovable-generated Vite + Nitro + TanStack app. 
// vite.config.ts — keep existing options, add the nitro section
import { defineConfig } from "@lovable.dev/vite-tanstack-config";

export default defineConfig({
  nitro: { preset: "node-server" },
});
web: node .output/server/index.mjs
scalingo create my-app
git add vite.config.ts Procfile && git commit -m "Migrate to scalingo"
git push && git push scalingo
  • Start with an M container. To leave Supabase, restore its backup or dump into a Scalingo PostgreSQL addon (512 MB or more).
  • Lovable's GitHub sync can overwrite Procfile and vite.config.ts; re-check both after each sync before pushing to Scalingo.

AI demos: Whisper, pgvector, OpenSearch RAG

All three are Demo pages. Sample code lives in <https://github.com/Scalingo/scalingo-labs>.

Speech to text with faster-whisper (<https://doc.scalingo.com/tutorials/whisper>, folder whisper-speech-to-text):

scalingo create my-whisper
scalingo --app my-whisper env-set MODEL_SIZE=small
git push scalingo main
MODEL_SIZEContainer
tiny, baseL
small (default)XL or 2XL
medium, large, turbo3XL

The model downloads on first boot; poll /health until status is ready. Transcription is synchronous; move it to a worker for long files.

Recommendations with pgvector (<https://doc.scalingo.com/tutorials/pgvector-recommendation>, folder filmrecommendation):

scalingo create my-filmreco
scalingo --app my-filmreco addons-add postgresql postgresql-starter-512
git push scalingo main
scalingo --app my-filmreco run python3 setup.py     # enables pgvector, creates and loads the table

pgvector is enabled with SQL (CREATE EXTENSION vector) from the one-off, not with a database feature toggle. One M web container is enough for the demo.

RAG retrieval with OpenSearch (<https://doc.scalingo.com/tutorials/opensearch-rag>): uses the bundled k-NN and ml-commons plugins on an OpenSearch addon (start at Starter 1024). Every call is a curl against $SCALINGO_OPENSEARCH_URL from a one-off:

  1. Cluster settings: plugins.ml_commons.only_run_on_ml_node=false, model_access_control_enabled=true, native_memory_threshold=99 (dev/test value).
  2. Register a model group, then huggingface/sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (TORCH_SCRIPT); poll the task for the model ID.
  3. Ingest pipeline with a text_embedding processor (passage_text → passage_embedding).
  4. Index with "knn": true, default_pipeline, and a 384-dimension knn_vector field.
  5. Hybrid search: neural + match queries combined with script_score.

$SCALINGO_OPENSEARCH_URL only exists inside the app's containers, so an unquoted scalingo run curl $SCALINGO_OPENSEARCH_URL... gets expanded (to nothing) by your local shell. Run the calls from an interactive one-off instead:

scalingo --app my-app run bash
# inside the container:
curl -s "$SCALINGO_OPENSEARCH_URL/_cluster/health"

Vector search is RAM- and CPU-hungry; size the plan to the knowledge base.

Elastic Stack (legacy)

(Demo, last updated February 2026) — Logstash + Kibana apps on top of the **Elasticsearch** addon, which Scalingo is phasing out in favour of OpenSearch. Prefer OpenSearch for new projects; use this recipe only to maintain an existing stack.
  • Logstash: repo Scalingo/logstash-scalingo (branch es7-compat), at least one L container, addons-add elasticsearch elasticsearch-starter-512 (plan as given by the tutorial; confirm with addons-plans elasticsearch), mandatory USER / PASSWORD for HTTP basic auth.
  • Ship another app's logs to it with a log drain: scalingo --app my-app log-drains-add --type elk --url <logstash-url>.
  • Kibana: BUILDPACK_URL=https://github.com/Scalingo/kibana-buildpack, ELASTICSEARCH_URL, plus ELASTICSEARCH_TLS_CA_URL if TLS is forced on the database.
  • Curator (index cleanup) runs on the Logstash app through a multi-buildpack (.buildpacks: JVM common, Python, Logstash, in that order) and the Scalingo Scheduler, which reads a cron.json at the repo root:
{
  "jobs": [
    { "command": "0 3,15 * * * curator --config curator.yml log-clean.yml" }
  ]
}

Scheduled jobs run as one-off containers; list them with scalingo --app my-app cron-tasks.
